1. Core Clinical Tension: A 45-year-old male with a history of recurrent febrile splenomegaly episodes over the preceding year presents with progressive wasting, epistaxis, profound pancytopenia, and massive splenomegaly extending to the right iliac fossa despite two prior courses of targeted parenteral therapy. The primary challenge is differentiating between refractory relapsed visceral protozoal infection, occult hematologic malignancy (such as myelodysplastic syndrome or leukemic infiltration), and chronic disseminated intracellular infections like tuberculosis or systemic mycoses.
2. Admission Breakpoint: The admission breakpoint occurs upon completion of emergency triage physical examination, baseline hematologic panel, metabolic and lipid profiles, abdominal ultrasonography, and plain radiography, prior to obtaining bone marrow aspiration cytology, rapid serologic antigen assays, or mycobacterial molecular amplification.
3. Differential Distinctions: Malaria is excluded by negative peripheral blood parasites. Sputum AFB and GeneXpert assays rule out pulmonary tuberculosis. Hematologic malignancy is distinguished by peripheral blood smear cytology revealing normal cellular morphology without circulating blasts or dysplasia, whereas visceral leishmaniasis is definitively established by bone marrow cytology demonstrating Leishman-Donovan bodies and positive rK39 serology.
case_prompt:
A 45-year-old male residing in Darchula District, Nepal, presents to a specialized tropical and infectious disease referral hospital with a 1-week history of intermittent fever and vague abdominal pain, accompanied by epistaxis for 4 days. Over the preceding twelve months, he experienced two previous hospital admissions for prolonged febrile illnesses associated with hepatosplenomegaly, which were treated with parenteral targeted antiparasitic courses.

On examination, the patient appears emaciated, pale, and markedly cachectic. Vital signs reveal a blood pressure of 90/60 mmHg, temperature of 96.2°F (35.7°C), and pulse rate of 84 beats per minute. Abdominal examination demonstrates massive splenomegaly crossing the midline and extending below the umbilicus down to the right iliac fossa.

Initial laboratory evaluation demonstrates severe pancytopenia: hemoglobin 5.8 g/dL, total leukocyte count 400/µL (69% neutrophils, 27% lymphocytes, 4% monocytes), and platelet count 29,000/µL. Peripheral blood smear reveals anisopoikilocytosis, hypochromic red blood cells, and markedly reduced white blood cells and platelets with normal cellular morphology and no abnormal or blast cells. Liver and metabolic testing shows serum albumin 1.0 g/dL, total protein 7.9 g/dL, prothrombin time 15 seconds (INR 1.3), and serum ferritin elevated at 766 ng/mL. Lipid panel reveals total cholesterol 67 mg/dL, triglycerides 136 mg/dL, HDL 20 mg/dL, and LDL 20 mg/dL. Plain chest radiography is unremarkable. Abdominal ultrasonography reveals massive splenomegaly measuring 26 cm, hepatomegaly with coarse echotexture, distended portal vein caliber with mild portal hypertension, minimal ascites, and no lymphadenopathy.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Intermittent fever and massive splenomegaly in an endemic area strongly suggest chronic malaria or hyperreactive malarial splenomegaly, but repeated peripheral blood parasite examinations were negative.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Malarial parasite and HIV serology were negative.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Tuberculosis was considered given cachexia, prolonged fevers, and hepatosplenomegaly, but chest imaging was normal and microbiological testing of sputum was negative.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Sputum for acid-fast bacilli was negative.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Profound pancytopenia with massive splenomegaly in an adult raised high concern for leukemia, myelodysplastic syndrome, or lymphoma, but peripheral blood smear cytology demonstrated normal cell morphology without blasts or abnormal cells.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Peripheral blood smear showed anisopoikilocytosis; hypochromic red blood cells; very low white blood cell count with normal morphology; no abnormal cells; and very low platelet count with normal morphology.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Demonstration of characteristic intracellular and extracellular Leishman-Donovan (LD) amastigotes on bone marrow cytology along with positive rK39 immunochromatographic testing confirmed relapsed visceral leishmaniasis.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Bone marrow cytology was performed which showed parasitic Leishman-Donovan (LD) bodies.

editor_comments: Distilled successfully following Stanford MedCaseReasoning methodology. Admission prompt strictly excludes post-admission bone marrow cytology, serological test names, and pathogen labels.
